meta.title: Advanced English Error Correction — 50 Mixed Grammar Questions (B2–C2)
meta.description: 50 error-correction questions that combine two or more advanced grammar topics (conditionals, inversion, subjunctive, passive, participle clauses, relative clauses, reported speech, comparison, ellipsis, articles, prepositions, and more). Click every incorrect part and type the correct form. Some items accept more than one correct answer.

multiErrorSegments.text: Had the committee been informed earlier,
if they were more cautious by nature,

details_explanation.explanation: The passage mixes a third conditional (past condition + past result) with a second conditional (present condition + present result). 'Had the committee been informed' is a correct inverted third-conditional if-clause, so its result must be 'would have postponed'. The second clause describes a present characteristic ('if they were more cautious by nature'), so its result must be present: 'would not occur'.
details_explanation.introduction: Mixed conditionals combine a condition in one time frame with a result in another. Inversion can replace 'if' in formal third-conditional clauses.

rules.title: 1. Third conditional with inversion
rules.explanation: Past unreal condition → past unreal result.
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle
notes: 'Had the committee been informed' = 'If the committee had been informed'.

rules.title: 2. Second conditional for present characteristics
rules.explanation: A present/general condition takes a present result.
rules.structure: If + subject + past simple, subject + would + base verb
notes: 'If they were more cautious by nature' describes a present trait.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I known, I would arrive earlier.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known, I would have arrived earlier.
common_mistakes.reason: A past condition requires a past result.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she were more careful, she would have made fewer mistakes now.
common_mistakes.correct: If she were more careful, she would make fewer mistakes now.
common_mistakes.reason: Present condition pairs with present result.

other_examples.sentence: Had the alarm been tested, the fire would not have spread.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya alarm diuji, kebakaran tidak akan menyebar.

other_examples.sentence: If he were more organised, he would not miss deadlines.
other_examples.translation: Jika dia lebih teratur, dia tidak akan melewatkan tenggat.

details_explanation.explanation: Three advanced structures interact here. (1) After 'It is essential that', English uses the mandative subjunctive: 'be submitted'. (2) 'Data' is a plural form in formal English, so 'have been verified'. (3) After the negative adverbial 'only after', the main clause requires subject–auxiliary inversion: 'should the findings be published'.
details_explanation.introduction: The mandative subjunctive, plural agreement with 'data', and negative-adverbial inversion are all formal features common in C1/C2 writing.

rules.title: 1. Mandative subjunctive
rules.explanation: After 'essential, vital, imperative, crucial that', use the base form of the verb.
rules.structure: It is essential that + subject + base verb
notes: No -s in the third person singular: 'that he submit'.

rules.title: 2. Inversion after 'only after'
rules.explanation: When 'only after' begins a clause, the following main clause inverts.
rules.structure: Only after + clause + auxiliary + subject + main verb
notes: 'should the findings be published' not 'the findings should be published'.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is vital that he is informed.
common_mistakes.correct: It is vital that he be informed.
common_mistakes.reason: Mandative subjunctive uses the base form.

common_mistakes.wrong: Only after the meeting he apologised.
common_mistakes.correct: Only after the meeting did he apologise.

other_examples.sentence: It is imperative that all candidates be interviewed.
other_examples.translation: Sangat penting bahwa semua kandidat diwawancarai.

other_examples.sentence: Only after the audit did the errors become apparent.
other_examples.translation: Hanya setelah audit kesalahan itu menjadi jelas.

multiErrorSegments.text: neither of the supervisors being aware

details_explanation.explanation: The opening participle clause is passive in meaning ('the team had been warned'), so it must be 'Having been warned'. The relative clause refers to 'the team', which is treated as a singular unit here, so 'which was responsible'. 'Neither of the supervisors being aware' is a correct absolute construction.
details_explanation.introduction: Perfect participle clauses can be active ('Having finished') or passive ('Having been warned'). Relative pronoun agreement depends on the noun the clause modifies.

rules.title: 1. Passive perfect participle
rules.explanation: Use 'having been + past participle' when the subject receives the action.
rules.structure: Having been + past participle, main clause
notes: 'Having warned' would mean the team did the warning.

rules.title: 2. Relative clause agreement
rules.explanation: The relative verb agrees with its antecedent.
notes: 'The team' as a unit takes a singular verb in this context.

common_mistakes.wrong: Having warned about the risks, the team proceeded.
common_mistakes.correct: Having been warned about the risks, the team proceeded.

common_mistakes.wrong: The team which were responsible.
common_mistakes.correct: The team which was responsible.

other_examples.sentence: Having been praised for her work, she felt encouraged.
other_examples.translation: Setelah dipuji atas karyanya, dia merasa terdorong.

other_examples.sentence: The committee, which was formed last year, meets monthly.
other_examples.translation: Komite, yang dibentuk tahun lalu, bertemu setiap bulan.

details_explanation.explanation: 'It was not until ... that ...' is a cleft structure referring to a completed past event, so the verb should be past simple: 'were noticed'. 'Never before' is a negative adverbial; when it starts a clause, inversion is required: 'had the board been'.
details_explanation.introduction: Cleft sentences focus information, while negative adverbials such as 'never before', 'seldom', and 'not only' trigger inversion.

rules.title: 1. 'It was not until' cleft
rules.explanation: The that-clause describes a past event and normally uses past simple.
rules.structure: It was not until + time + that + past simple
notes: 'have been noticed' wrongly links a past event to present relevance.

rules.title: 2. Negative adverbial inversion
rules.explanation: After 'never before', put the auxiliary before the subject.
rules.structure: Never before + auxiliary + subject + past participle
notes: 'had the board been' not 'the board had been'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Never before the board had been so unprepared.
common_mistakes.correct: Never before had the board been so unprepared.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was not until yesterday that I have realised.
common_mistakes.correct: It was not until yesterday that I realised.

other_examples.sentence: It was not until midnight that the guests left.
other_examples.translation: Baru tengah malam para tamu pergi.

other_examples.sentence: Never before had she seen such a sight.
other_examples.translation: Belum pernah sebelumnya dia melihat pemandangan seperti itu.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Recommend' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive: 'recommended postponing'. The list must also be parallel, so all three items should be gerunds: 'postponing ... revising ... informing'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some verbs take gerund complements (recommend, suggest, enjoy), and lists require parallel grammatical forms.

rules.title: 1. Gerund after 'recommend'
rules.explanation: Use the -ing form when no object is mentioned.
notes: 'recommend that somebody do' is also possible, but not 'recommend to do'.

rules.title: 2. Parallelism in lists
rules.explanation: Items joined by 'and' should have the same form.
notes: Mixing infinitives and gerunds breaks parallelism.

common_mistakes.wrong: She recommended to take a break.
common_mistakes.correct: She recommended taking a break.

common_mistakes.wrong: He likes swimming, hiking, and to camp.
common_mistakes.correct: He likes swimming, hiking, and camping.

other_examples.sentence: The doctor recommended reducing salt and exercising daily.
other_examples.translation: Dokter menyarankan mengurangi garam dan berolahraga setiap hari.

other_examples.sentence: She enjoys reading, painting, and travelling.
other_examples.translation: Dia menikmati membaca, melukis, dan bepergian.

details_explanation.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, 'will' shifts to 'would'. Time expressions also shift: 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' or 'the following day'. The past perfect continuous 'had been working' is correctly retained because it describes an earlier ongoing action.
details_explanation.introduction: Reported speech requires backshift of tenses and adjustments to time and place references.

rules.title: 1. Backshift of modal 'will'
rules.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would'.
notes: No backshift if the situation is still true, but standard reporting shifts it.

rules.title: 2. Time expression shift
rules.explanation: 'Tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' or 'the following day'.
rules.structure: tomorrow → the next day / the following day

common_mistakes.wrong: He said he will come tomorrow.
common_mistakes.correct: He said he would come the next day.
common_mistakes.reason: Backshift and time shift are required.

common_mistakes.wrong: She said she had finished it yesterday.
common_mistakes.correct: She said she had finished it the day before.

other_examples.sentence: He told me he would call the following week.
other_examples.translation: Dia memberitahuku dia akan menelepon minggu berikutnya.

other_examples.sentence: They said they had already eaten.
other_examples.translation: Mereka mengatakan mereka sudah makan.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject of the main clause is 'the number', which is singular, so 'has increased'. Inside the relative clause, 'who' refers to 'students' (plural), so 'have enrolled'. This is a classic agreement trap involving quantity expressions.
details_explanation.introduction: 'The number of' takes a singular verb, while 'a number of' takes a plural verb. Relative pronouns agree with their antecedent.

rules.title: 1. 'The number of' + singular verb
rules.explanation: The head noun is 'number', not the plural noun after 'of'.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: 'A number of students are' is different: here 'a number of' means 'many'.

rules.title: 2. Relative pronoun agreement
rules.explanation: 'Who' refers to 'students', so the relative verb is plural.

common_mistakes.wrong: The number of cars have risen.
common_mistakes.correct: The number of cars has risen.

common_mistakes.wrong: The students who has registered.
common_mistakes.correct: The students who have registered.
common_mistakes.reason: Relative verb agrees with plural antecedent.

other_examples.sentence: The number of applicants has doubled.
other_examples.translation: Jumlah pelamar telah berlipat ganda.

other_examples.sentence: A number of issues have been raised.
other_examples.translation: Sejumlah masalah telah diangkat.

correctAnswers: but she also refused to accept

details_explanation.explanation: 'Insist' is followed by the preposition 'on': 'insist on paying'. 'Refuse' takes a to-infinitive: 'refused to accept'. The inverted 'Not only did she insist' is correctly formed.
details_explanation.introduction: Verb + preposition collocations and verb complement patterns must be memorised; errors here are common at advanced levels.

rules.title: 1. 'Insist on' + gerund
rules.explanation: Insist is followed by 'on' and a gerund.

rules.title: 2. 'Refuse' + to-infinitive
rules.explanation: Refuse takes a to-infinitive, not a gerund.
notes: 'Refuse accepting' is incorrect in standard English.

common_mistakes.wrong: She insisted in coming.
common_mistakes.correct: She insisted on coming.

common_mistakes.wrong: He refused going.
common_mistakes.correct: He refused to go.

other_examples.sentence: They insisted on checking every detail.
other_examples.translation: Mereka bersikeras memeriksa setiap detail.

other_examples.sentence: She refused to sign the contract.

correctAnswers: than that of the previous administration,
and it could have been implemented

details_explanation.explanation: The comparison is between 'the new policy' and 'the policy of the previous administration', so we need 'that of' to avoid comparing a policy with an administration. The unreal past situation requires a modal perfect: 'could have been implemented'.
details_explanation.introduction: Comparison must be logically parallel, often using 'that of/those of'. Modal perfects express unrealised past possibilities.

rules.title: 1. Comparative substitution with 'that of'
rules.explanation: Use 'that of' to compare a singular noun with a matching noun phrase.
rules.structure: noun + be + comparative + than that of + noun
notes: 'Those of' is used for plural nouns.

rules.title: 2. Modal perfect for unreal past
rules.explanation: 'Could have + past participle' expresses a past possibility that did not happen.
notes: The inverted condition 'had the resources been available' is correct.

common_mistakes.wrong: The weather here is better than London.
common_mistakes.correct: The weather here is better than that of London.

common_mistakes.wrong: It could be done earlier.
common_mistakes.correct: It could have been done earlier.
common_mistakes.reason: Past unreal possibility needs modal perfect.

other_examples.sentence: Their results were better than those of their rivals.
other_examples.translation: Hasil mereka lebih baik daripada hasil para pesaing.

other_examples.sentence: The accident could have been avoided.
other_examples.translation: Kecelakaan itu bisa saja dihindari.

details_explanation.explanation: The head noun is 'implementation' (singular), so 'has been delayed'. 'Stakeholders' is plural, so 'were consulted'. Nominalised subjects often hide the true head noun, causing agreement errors.
details_explanation.introduction: Nominalisation turns verbs or adjectives into nouns. Identify the head noun to choose the correct verb agreement.

rules.title: 1. Agreement with nominalised subjects
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the head noun, not with the noun in the prepositional phrase.
rules.structure: The implementation of + plural noun + singular verb

rules.title: 2. Agreement with 'stakeholders'
rules.explanation: Plural countable nouns take plural verbs.

common_mistakes.wrong: The development of these tools have changed everything.
common_mistakes.correct: The development of these tools has changed everything.

common_mistakes.wrong: The staff was informed.
common_mistakes.correct: The staff were informed.
common_mistakes.reason: In British English 'staff' often takes a plural verb.

other_examples.sentence: The introduction of new rules has caused confusion.

other_examples.sentence: The employees were consulted before the change.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Should you require' is a correct inverted conditional (= 'If you should require'). 'It is imperative that' requires the mandative subjunctive 'be completed'. 'Under no circumstances' is a negative adverbial, so the following clause inverts: 'should late applications be accepted'.
details_explanation.introduction: This item combines three formal structures: inverted conditionals, the mandative subjunctive, and negative-adverbial inversion.

rules.title: 1. Inverted conditional with 'should'
rules.explanation: 'Should + subject + verb' replaces 'if + subject + should + verb'.
rules.structure: Should + subject + base verb, main clause
notes: Common in formal and polite writing.

rules.title: 2. Mandative subjunctive
rules.explanation: After 'imperative that', use the base form.
rules.structure: It is imperative that + subject + base verb

rules.title: 3. Negative adverbial inversion
rules.explanation: 'Under no circumstances' triggers auxiliary–subject inversion.
rules.structure: Under no circumstances + auxiliary + subject + verb

common_mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances you should smoke.
common_mistakes.correct: Under no circumstances should you smoke.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is vital that he is present.
common_mistakes.correct: It is vital that he be present.
common_mistakes.reason: Mandative subjunctive uses the base form.

other_examples.sentence: Should you need help, please call.
other_examples.translation: Jika Anda membutuhkan bantuan, silakan menelepon.

other_examples.sentence: Under no circumstances should the door be left open.
other_examples.translation: Dalam keadaan apa pun pintu tidak boleh dibiarkan terbuka.

multiErrorSegments.text: had been funded by the government,

details_explanation.explanation: 'Who's' is the contraction of 'who is' or 'who has'; the possessive relative pronoun is 'whose'. The perfect participle is active here because the scientist did the dedicating: 'having dedicated'.
details_explanation.introduction: Distinguish 'who's' from 'whose', and choose active or passive perfect participles according to who performs the action.

rules.title: 1. 'Whose' as possessive relative
rules.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession and replaces 'his/her/its/their'.

rules.title: 2. Active perfect participle
rules.explanation: Use 'having + past participle' when the subject performs the action.

common_mistakes.wrong: The man who's car was stolen.
common_mistakes.correct: The man whose car was stolen.

common_mistakes.wrong: Having been finished the work, she left.
common_mistakes.correct: Having finished the work, she left.

other_examples.sentence: The author whose book won the prize was interviewed.
other_examples.translation: Penulis yang bukunya memenangkan hadiah diwawancarai.

other_examples.sentence: Having completed the course, he applied for a job.
other_examples.translation: Setelah menyelesaikan kursus, dia melamar pekerjaan.

multiErrorSegments.text: I could not help but to be
correctAnswers: I could not help but be

details_explanation.explanation: The inverted third conditional 'Had I known' requires 'would have arrived'. The idiom 'cannot help' is followed by a bare infinitive ('but be') or a gerund ('being'), not 'but to be'.
details_explanation.introduction: Fixed expressions such as 'cannot help but' have strict complement patterns that often cause errors.

rules.title: 1. Third conditional result
rules.explanation: Past unreal condition → would have + past participle.
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle
notes: 'I would arrive' describes a present/future result.

rules.title: 2. 'Cannot help' patterns
rules.explanation: Two correct patterns exist.
rules.structure: cannot help but + base verb / cannot help + verb-ing
notes: 'Cannot help but to be' is incorrect.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I seen him, I would tell him.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I seen him, I would have told him.

common_mistakes.wrong: I couldn't help but to laugh.
common_mistakes.correct: I couldn't help but laugh.

other_examples.sentence: Had we left earlier, we would have caught the train.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya kami berangkat lebih awal, kami akan menangkap kereta.

other_examples.sentence: She couldn't help laughing at the joke.
other_examples.translation: Dia tidak bisa menahan tawa pada lelucon itu.

details_explanation.explanation: The causative structure 'have something done' requires a past participle: 'had the report rewritten'. The subject 'the final version' is singular, so 'was sent'.
details_explanation.introduction: Causative 'have' and passive voice both use past participles, but agreement in the passive must match the subject.

rules.title: 1. Causative 'have + object + past participle'
rules.explanation: Use the past participle for the action done by someone else.
notes: 'Had the report rewritten' = arranged for it to be rewritten.

rules.title: 2. Passive agreement
rules.explanation: The passive auxiliary agrees with the subject.

common_mistakes.wrong: I had my hair cutted.
common_mistakes.correct: I had my hair cut.
common_mistakes.reason: Use the past participle, not a regularised form.

common_mistakes.wrong: The documents was signed.
common_mistakes.correct: The documents were signed.

other_examples.sentence: She had her car repaired.
other_examples.translation: Dia menyuruh mobilnya diperbaiki.

other_examples.sentence: The letter was sent yesterday.
other_examples.translation: Surat itu dikirim kemarin.

multiErrorSegments.text: She is accustomed to work late
correctAnswers: She is accustomed to working late

multiErrorSegments.text: and prefers to finish her tasks

details_explanation.explanation: 'Accustomed to' is a prepositional phrase followed by a gerund: 'accustomed to working'. 'What' cannot serve as a non-defining relative pronoun referring to a whole clause; use 'which'.
details_explanation.introduction: Adjective + preposition combinations often require gerunds. 'Which' can refer to a whole preceding clause; 'what' cannot.

rules.title: 1. 'Accustomed to' + gerund
rules.explanation: 'To' here is a preposition, not an infinitive marker.
notes: Similarly: 'look forward to seeing', 'be used to waking'.

rules.title: 2. Sentential relative 'which'
rules.explanation: Use 'which' to comment on the whole previous clause.
notes: 'What' is a fused relative pronoun and cannot do this.

common_mistakes.wrong: I am used to wake up early.
common_mistakes.correct: I am used to waking up early.

common_mistakes.wrong: He arrived late, what annoyed us.
common_mistakes.correct: He arrived late, which annoyed us.

other_examples.sentence: She is accustomed to working under pressure.
other_examples.translation: Dia terbiasa bekerja di bawah tekanan.

other_examples.sentence: He forgot the meeting, which was unfortunate.
other_examples.translation: Dia lupa rapat itu, yang sayang sekali.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Had it not been for' introduces a past unreal condition, so the result must be 'would have failed'. 'It is crucial that' triggers the mandative subjunctive: 'be informed'.
details_explanation.introduction: Formal writing frequently combines inverted conditionals with mandative subjunctive clauses.

rules.title: 1. 'Had it not been for' + would have
rules.explanation: This idiom introduces a past counterfactual.
rules.structure: Had it not been for + noun, subject + would have + past participle

rules.title: 2. Mandative subjunctive after 'crucial'
rules.explanation: Use the base form in the that-clause.
rules.structure: It is crucial that + subject + base verb

common_mistakes.wrong: Had it not been for you, I would fail.
common_mistakes.correct: Had it not been for you, I would have failed.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is crucial that she is aware.
common_mistakes.correct: It is crucial that she be aware.

other_examples.sentence: Had it not been for the delay, we would have arrived on time.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya bukan karena penundaan, kami akan tiba tepat waktu.

other_examples.sentence: It is crucial that everyone be notified.
other_examples.translation: Sangat penting bahwa semua orang diberi tahu.

multiErrorSegments.text: is larger than any city in Japan,
correctAnswers: is larger than that of any other city in Japan,

details_explanation.explanation: A population cannot be larger than a city; it is larger than 'that of' another city. Also, 'Tokyo' must be excluded from the comparison, so 'any other city'. The transport system is singular, so 'that of', not 'those of'.
details_explanation.introduction: Comparatives require logically parallel elements and correct singular/plural substitution (that of / those of).

rules.title: 1. 'That of' / 'those of' substitution
rules.explanation: Use 'that of' for singular and 'those of' for plural nouns.
rules.structure: noun + be + comparative + than that of / those of + noun
notes: Population → that of; systems → those of.

rules.title: 2. Excluding the subject from comparison
rules.explanation: Use 'other' when the subject belongs to the same group.
rules.structure: comparative + than any other + singular noun
notes: Tokyo is itself a city in Japan.

common_mistakes.wrong: His salary is higher than his brother.
common_mistakes.correct: His salary is higher than that of his brother.

common_mistakes.wrong: She is taller than any girl in the class.
common_mistakes.correct: She is taller than any other girl in the class.
common_mistakes.reason: She is in the class; exclude her.

other_examples.sentence: The climate of Kyoto is milder than that of Sapporo.
other_examples.translation: Iklim Kyoto lebih sejuk daripada iklim Sapporo.

other_examples.sentence: Their prices are lower than those of their competitors.
other_examples.translation: Harga mereka lebih rendah daripada harga para pesaing.

details_explanation.explanation: A specific past time ('in the 12th century') requires past simple, not present perfect: 'was written'. After the past reporting verb 'claimed', the earlier state must be past perfect: 'had been preserved'.
details_explanation.introduction: Passive reporting structures and reported speech both require careful tense selection.

rules.title: 1. Specific past time → past simple
rules.explanation: Finished past time expressions do not take the present perfect.
notes: 'In the 12th century' is a finished past time.

rules.title: 2. Backshift after a past reporting verb
rules.explanation: An earlier situation is expressed with the past perfect.
rules.structure: claimed that + had been + past participle
notes: The preservation happened before the claim.

common_mistakes.wrong: The letter has been written in 1999.
common_mistakes.correct: The letter was written in 1999.
common_mistakes.reason: Specific past time takes past simple.

common_mistakes.wrong: He said it has been done.
common_mistakes.correct: He said it had been done.

other_examples.sentence: It is said that the bridge was built in 1800.
other_examples.translation: Dikatakan bahwa jembatan itu dibangun pada 1800.

other_examples.sentence: They claimed the painting had been stolen.
other_examples.translation: Mereka mengklaim lukisan itu telah dicuri.

details_explanation.explanation: When 'only if' starts a sentence, the main clause requires inversion: 'can we proceed'. 'It is vital that' requires the mandative subjunctive: 'be reviewed'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Only if' and 'only when' are negative-like adverbials that trigger inversion in the main clause.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after 'only if'
rules.explanation: The main clause inverts; the if-clause does not.
rules.structure: Only if + clause + auxiliary + subject + verb

rules.title: 2. Mandative subjunctive
rules.explanation: After 'vital that', use the base form.
rules.structure: It is vital that + subject + base verb

common_mistakes.wrong: Only if you study you will pass.
common_mistakes.correct: Only if you study will you pass.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is vital that the report is checked.
common_mistakes.correct: It is vital that the report be checked.

other_examples.sentence: Only if we leave now can we catch the train.
other_examples.translation: Hanya jika kita berangkat sekarang kita bisa menangkap kereta.

other_examples.sentence: It is vital that all safety checks be completed.
